items.question: Why do you think now is the time to bring diffusion language models into production?
items.object: Diffusion language models for production deployment
items.answer: If you need to scale up these models and they are actually getting into production, the price per token or the watts needed per token becomes the key metric that you care about. items.question: Why did you find diffusion models promising as an alternative to GANs and autoregressive models for generating images?
items.object: Diffusion models as an alternative to GANs and autoregressive image generation
items.answer: Back then, the field was dominated by GANs, generative adversarial networks. That's the old approach where there's two neural networks. There is one that generates images and there's one that's trying to discriminate and figure out if the images are real or fake, and then you train them one against each other. It's a very unstable and challenging optimization problem because there's this game-theoretic aspect to it where they need to outcompete each other, these two neural networks, and it was very unstable, very difficult to get it to work well. Lots of tricks were needed. We were trying in my lab to experiment with alternatives. One alternative was the usual auto-regressive approach where you generate the image, let's say, one pixel at a time, and that's never worked particularly well for images and video, and it still doesn't. It's just very slow and not very accurate. We came up with this alternative approach which is now called a diffusion model, where essentially you generate an image by starting from noise and then iteratively refining it until you get a crisp, nice image that's consistent with the prompt at the end. The key benefit is that the training objective is very stable. The neural network is trying to just denoise an image. You take images, add noise, and train a neural network to remove noise. It's a fairly standard, relatively easy optimization problem that you can use to train neural networks over large datasets, and it works reasonably well. You can then use this neural network at inference time to generate images because the networks have been trained to remove noise, improve the samples, correct mistakes. It turns out that you can just start with pure noise and then apply this denoising network a bunch of times, and at the end you get a really nice image.

items.question: How do you connect the appeal of diffusion models' inference computation to today's interest in chains of thought in LLMs?
items.object: Cheap training with powerful inference in diffusion models and LLMs
items.answer: Back then people were not thinking about test-time inference and those kinds of things, but one of the reasons we really wanted to get this to work was that it had the flavor of a neural network where you have a very deep inference path, where you're chaining together many evaluations of this neural network at inference time. You have a very deep computation graph that can do very powerful things, but it's still very scalable during training because you don't have to unroll all of this computation during training. During training, you just train the model to remove noise. You basically need a single neural network evaluation during training. This idea of having something that is cheap to train, yet very powerful at inference time, has always been on the back of my mind: trying to think about ways to do these sorts of computations efficiently, which is now showing up in a different form in the context of LLMs, where people are very excited about chains of thought and being able to adjust the amount of compute at inference time. I feel like it's a similar idea, although implemented on top of a very different kind of generative model.

items.question: Why do you see the discrete nature of text and code as a challenge for diffusion models?
items.object: The challenge of applying diffusion models to discrete text and code
items.answer: If I think about an image or just even a single pixel, it's a bunch of colors, and the interesting thing is that if you change the colors a little bit, the meaning doesn't change. In particular, you can think about two possible colors for a pixel, and all the things in between them still make sense and they don't change the meaning of the image in any dramatic way. But if you think about text and you take two words, then it's not clear what's in between the meaning of two different words. There is no real geometry to the space of possible tokens or words. That makes the idea of denoising much more challenging, because it's not clear what it means to perturb the noise to text. The whole geometry does not exist. A lot of the concepts that were defined for and invented to get diffusion models to work on images and video were relying very heavily on the fact that there is some kind of continuum of possible images and you can interpolate between them, and it makes sense to get the model to smoothly move from one image to another. In the context of text and code, everything is very discrete, so it's not obvious how the mathematics developed for continuous spaces translates immediately to discrete spaces.

items.question: What do you see as the main difficulty with building diffusion models for language generation in embedding space?

items.answer: There are approaches that try to build diffusion models for language generation in the embedding space, where you embed everything and build a diffusion model. The problem is that eventually you have to decode back to text. I cannot give an embedding to my users or my customers. At the end of the day, the diffusion model will make some small mistakes, and it might not end up exactly in a space, at a point that corresponds to one of the existing words in the dictionary. items.question: What do you see as the key result of your lab’s paper comparing diffusion and autoregressive training for language generation?
items.object: Ermon’s lab’s academic comparison of diffusion and autoregressive language models
items.answer: The initial results were still in the academic setting. It was again from my lab, where we had a paper a couple of years ago essentially showing that for the first time it was possible to train a transformer-based model. You basically took a GPT-2-size model and trained it auto-regressively the usual way, to predict the next token, the way everybody else is training LLMs, and you can train the same neural network as a diffusion model. In that paper we showed that for the first time we were able to match the quality. In terms of perplexity and the quality of the text these two models are able to generate, it was about the same, but the diffusion model was significantly faster. items.question: How do you think about making a fair comparison between diffusion and auto-regressive language models?
items.object: Comparing diffusion and auto-regressive language modeling
items.answer: It's really just almost like an A/B test, a very fair comparison. You take the same exact neural network architecture with the same number of parameters, train it on the same amount of data. You train it on the one hand as a typical auto-regressive model, where you just predict the next token, and that's how you use it at inference time. On the other hand, you can train it as a diffusion model. At that point, the difference in performance is entirely due to the different modeling paradigm, diffusion versus auto-regressive.

items.question: How do you understand token masking as a way to train diffusion language models?
items.object: Token masking as a noise process for diffusion language models
items.answer: At an intuitive level, it's all somewhat similar in the sense that there is still a neural network trained to remove noise. It's just that the noise process is no longer adding small numbers to the pixel intensities. There are different kinds of noise processes that you can use. One that works pretty well is basically one where you mask out tokens. You hide them. You take a sentence and remove some of the tokens; you hide them from the neural network and ask the neural network, can you predict what those tokens were? It's similar in some sense to next-token prediction, except that things are done out of order and the network needs to use context to the left and to the right, and combine it in interesting ways to figure out how to predict all these missing tokens from the sentence.

items.question: How do you explain the efficiency advantage of diffusion language models over autoregressive generation?
items.object: The efficiency advantage of diffusion language models
items.answer: In that ICML paper that I mentioned, we showed that once you can predict some of the missing tokens, you can also generate content from scratch, because you can start with a sentence where everything is masked and then let the neural network figure out how to fill in pieces, but it does so out of order. Instead of generating left to right one token at a time, it does it in any order, and crucially the network can output more than one token at a time. That's why these models are so much faster, because in the auto-regressive world, if you want to generate a thousand tokens, you need a thousand neural network evaluations. In the context of a diffusion language model, the neural network can output many tokens at every step, and to the extent that you don't need too many steps, 20 denoising steps, these models can be much more efficient.

items.question: Why do you find controlling the number of denoising steps in a diffusion language model exciting as a way to scale inference-time compute?
items.object: Test-time scaling through denoising steps in diffusion language models
items.answer: For sure, this idea of being able to control the quality of the answer as a function of the number of improvement steps, the number of denoising steps, is very exciting because it gives you another direction to do test-time scaling, test-time inference, using compute at inference time to control the quality of your answers. With an auto-regressive model the only way you can control the quality of the answer is by producing a longer thinking trace. That's what these reasoning models are doing: they produce a thinking trace before providing the right answer, and the longer you let them think, the better usually the quality of the answer is, and the more expensive and slower it becomes. A diffusion language model has a different kind of access to do something similar, where you can control the number of denoising steps, the number of iterations. The more iterations you do, the higher the quality becomes, but all the edits are essentially happening in place. You don't necessarily have to make the trace longer; the model is able to do error correction, improve its own answer without having to make it longer and longer, which saves memory and is significantly more efficient.

items.answer: There are many different ways of handling outputs of variable length. We have figured out a way to do it at Inception. I'm sure there are other ways; there's also the idea of doing rolling blocks, which also makes sense and has been published in the literature. There are different ways of handling variable length. It's possible to do it with a diffusion language model. It does not affect the scaling with respect to context size. items.question: How do you think about adapting existing language-model training techniques to diffusion language models?
items.object: Adapting training techniques to diffusion language models
items.answer: Some do; some we had to reinvent from scratch. If you think about pre-training, mid-training, SFT, a lot of that is relatively simple in the sense that you can essentially use the same kinds of datasets. The architectures don't have to change too much, and you just need to change the loss function essentially, from next-token prediction to denoising. I think about reinforcement learning: that's where things become more interesting. In the context of reinforcement learning, whether you do it from human preferences or have some kind of verifiable or non-verifiable reward to optimize for, the sampling process is quite different, and so the way you would propagate that information back into the network is different. In fact, it's beneficial to diffusion language models because in the context of RL post-training the real bottleneck is inference. If you're doing RL post-training of an LLM, you're going to spend most of your time doing rollouts. You get the model to provide candidate solutions, score them using your reward function, and then figure out how to teach the model to do better, to put more probability mass on the rollouts that were good and avoid rollouts that were not good as evaluated by the reward function. Because diffusion language models are so much faster at inference time, you can do different things in the RL post-training stage. That's where we're spending a lot of our time right now: figuring out the right way to do RL post-training for a diffusion model.

items.question: How do you think about reusing a pretrained autoregressive model to train a diffusion language model?
items.object: Reusing pretrained autoregressive models to train diffusion language models
items.answer: There have been a number of papers in the academic literature trying out various recipes for doing exactly that. To some extent embeddings can still be reused, and to some extent networks. The real challenge is that the attention mask you use in a traditional auto-regressive model is causal, so the model only knows how to use context to the left as it figures out what to do next. In a diffusion language model, you really want to be able to have access to the context to the left and to the right as you decide what to change. It's one of the key properties that make these models potentially much higher quality compared to auto-regressive models. That's the challenging bit. People have explored ways of annealing the attention mask to make it go from causal to something non-causal slowly, making the model drift away from the initial auto-regressive state. There are more mathematically sophisticated ways of converting the likelihood from an auto-regressive model to a score function, which is what you need in a diffusion model. More broadly, one thing that always works is that you can get samples from the auto-regressive model. That's usually a good way to generate synthetic data that you can use to train your diffusion language model. That's almost like a black box that you can always use to combine and try to get knowledge out of an existing model. With the Distil-Whistle, I think that's been on the mind of a lot of labs and researchers, and it seems to be going on at pretty massive scales in other places, but that's always possible.

items.question: Why do you see serving infrastructure as a challenge for putting diffusion language models into production?
items.object: Serving infrastructure for diffusion language models
items.answer: I think it's one of the reasons why there are still no other providers able to serve diffusion language models in production today. If you think about vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT, these frameworks that exist, and that are open source, they're really good at serving auto-regressive LLMs efficiently. They handle things like continuous batching: when there is a stream of requests coming in, how do you batch them together to serve them efficiently? There are all kinds of optimizations you need to do once you have access to multiple GPUs and many requests. A lot of existing frameworks and great work have been done for auto-regressive models. items.question: How do you judge Mercury 2's competitive position against frontier-lab language models?
items.object: Mercury 2's competitive position and quality limitations
items.answer: The result is that our latest diffusion language model, Mercury 2, is comparable in quality, about the same as the speed-optimized models from Frontier Labs, Haiku, Mini, Flash models, but significantly faster, 5–10x faster depending on which one you compare against. The big limitation is that it's not the highest possible quality. If you want the most intelligent model, like the latest Opus model or the latest Pro model from Google's Gemini Pro, we're not at that quality level. We have not yet trained a diffusion language model that matches the quality of the best models from Frontier Labs. That's the key limitation at the moment. We've been able to show that we can shift the Pareto frontier of quality versus speed at the level of the speed-optimized models from Frontier Labs, but we need to do more work to keep increasing the quality of our models, train bigger diffusion language models, use more data, figure out better training techniques to close that gap. At that point, we would have something really valuable.

items.question: What do you see as the main open scientific questions in diffusion language models?
items.object: Open scientific questions in diffusion language models
items.answer: It's still pretty open in terms of what is the best way to train one of these models. What is the denoising process? There are many choices there. We have some things that work, but there could be better ones. If you think about inference, the interesting thing about diffusion language models is that training and inference are decoupled. In an auto-regressive model, you train to predict the next token, and at inference time the only thing you can do is reuse exactly the same process over and over. In a diffusion language model, you're essentially solving a differential equation to generate samples. For image and video generation, there are many methods you can use to accelerate sampling. Numerical-method techniques like fancy ODE, ordinary differential equation solvers, or stochastic differential equation solvers have been ported over to machine learning and led to really fast, high-quality sampling algorithms for traditional continuous diffusion models. The space of discrete language diffusion models is still the Wild West. Nobody knows the best way to do things. Architecture-wise, I think there's still a lot that can be changed. If you think about RL, what is the right way to do RL using a diffusion language model? Even for traditional image and video models, there's still a lot of research wide open: what's the best way to incorporate information through the diffusion process? What's the most efficient way of doing it? I'm still involved through my lab at Stanford in some research projects, some collaborations with Nvidia where we're training big video models, Cosmos. We've been working at figuring out the right recipe for RL on these more standard diffusion models that have been around for six or seven years. The space for language, discrete, is still much less mature, and there is a lot of research to be done there as well.

items.question: How do you assess our scientific understanding of generalization in deep learning?
items.object: Scientific understanding of generalization in deep learning
items.answer: We're learning from limited data. We need this model to generalize, and generalization is very, very, very poorly understood. Nobody really understands how generalization in deep learning works. Even for classification, very smart people in ML theory have spent a lot of time trying to understand how generalization works in deep learning. The progress has been very limited. To this day, there is no predictive theory that can tell you, "Will this neural network generalize?" It's all very empirical. You have to try, and then see, did it work or not? There is no theory at any reasonable scale that people would care about that is predictive and would tell you how well a neural network would work in practice, even for classification. For generation, generative models, it's even worse. It's a problem that fundamentally should be impossible to solve. There is a curse of dimensionality. There are some pretty good arguments for why what these models are doing should not be possible, yet they work. items.question: Why do you see controllable generation as an exciting direction for diffusion language models?
items.object: Controllable generation with diffusion models
items.answer: One interesting direction that I think is exciting, and also practically relevant, is controllability. People care about being able to control the outputs of these models, and usually that's done through a prompt, maybe some guardrails at the end. There is a certain stack and a certain set of things you can and cannot do with an auto-regressive model. A diffusion model, at least for images, is known to be much more suitable for controllable generation. The reason is that because the object, let's say the image you're generating, is available to the model from the very beginning, it's very easy for the model to check whether this object it's generating is consistent with some constraints or a control signal that you want to use to make sure the output is consistent with whatever you want the model to generate. You can check whether it matches your conditions, and you can also steer the generation process in a direction that makes it consistent with external constraints. That's only possible because you have the full object from the very beginning, as opposed to generating token by token, where you can only check whether it satisfies the constraint at the end. That's why diffusion models have been used a lot as priors for solving inverse problems in medical imaging. There are applications where this ability to control the output through some external signal has been important. I saw some papers where we're doing medical imaging. The idea is that when you do a CT scan, you're taking projections of your body cross-section and trying to reconstruct what your body looks like from measurements you get from the machine. The more measurements you get, the higher the quality of the reconstruction, but it also means more radiation for the patient. If you had a good prior model of what the body looks like, which can be given by a diffusion model, you can force the model to produce something likely to correspond to an actual human body, but also consistent with the measurements you're getting for this particular patient. That can significantly reduce the number of measurements you need to take for the same quality level, which means less radiation for the patients. There are a number of problems with that flavor where diffusion models have been really good. How to do that for text? There's some work there, but it'd be pretty exciting, because people care about being able to stay on brand and, of course, safety constraints. There's a bunch of settings where you want to control the output of the model. I think that's an exciting possibility that's pretty unique to diffusion language models.

items.answer: What's exciting is that it's unlikely one architecture is going to dominate the other one. items.question: How do you assess Google's position in bringing Gemini Diffusion to production compared with a focused startup like yours?
items.object: Google's Gemini Diffusion and the organizational challenges of bringing an alternative model architecture to production
items.answer: I don't have any inside information in terms of what they're doing, but as you said, they also announced a diffusion language model, Gemini Diffusion, a few months after we announced our first Mercury model. I'd like to think that maybe that had a little bit of influence and impact there, pushing them to actually show they have something too. What they published back then, those numbers were very comparable to our initial Mercury 1 model. I don't know whether they've been able to improve. What I know is that it's not yet in production and it's not yet available to customers. I'm guessing they've maybe not figured out, or they're still working on figuring out, how to serve it efficiently and what the best use cases are. My sense is that there is a big switching cost. They're very focused on Gemini and their main model. That could be the issue with these big labs: they're only in one direction, and it's hard for them to really focus on an alternative direction. As a startup, we're much better positioned to do that because we're laser-focused on one thing and we can deliver and build everything that's needed to get that technology to succeed. items.question: Why do you find diffusion language models exciting as a research direction?
